questions.text: What is the Modulus of Elasticity for structural steel, and does it vary with steel grade?

options.text: E varies significantly (from 180,000 to 220,000 MPa) based on the carbon content and alloy of the steel grade
E = 200,000 MPa for all structural steel grades; grade designation specifies Fy and Fu, not E
E = 200,000 MPa only for A36; higher strength grades like Grade 50 have higher E values to resist deflection
E is not a material property; it depends entirely on the thickness and geometry of the member

rationale.a: E is a constant material property of steel and does not fluctuate with grade designations[cite: 1].
rationale.c: Higher strength steel allows for higher loads before yielding, but it does not change the initial stiffness (slope of the elastic region)[cite: 1].
rationale.d: E is an intrinsic material property; geometry determines the moment of inertia (I), not the modulus of elasticity[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: E = 200,000 MPa (200 GPa) is considered a material constant for all structural steel grades. While yield strength (Fy) and ultimate strength (Fu) vary by grade, the stiffness (E) does not[cite: 1].
rationale.takeaway: Structural steel E is constant at 200,000 MPa regardless of grade[cite: 1].

questions.text: Two reinforced concrete beams have the same span and loading. Beam A uses f'c = 25 MPa; Beam B uses f'c = 40 MPa. If both have the same gross moment of inertia (Ig), how do their deflections compare?

options.text: Beam B deflects 60% more because higher strength allows for more flexibility
Beam A deflects more because it has lower E; the ratio of deflections is approximately 1.27:1
Both beams deflect the same amount because deflection depends only on Ig, not f'c
Beam B deflects 1.6 times less because strength is directly proportional to deflection

rationale.a: Higher strength concrete is stiffer, meaning it deflects less, not more[cite: 1].
rationale.c: Deflection calculation (δ = kPL³/EI) requires the Modulus of Elasticity (E), which changes with f'c[cite: 1].
rationale.d: Strength (f'c) is not linearly proportional to deflection; it is related via the square root in the E calculation[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: Deflection is inversely proportional to E. Ec(25) = 4700√25 = 23,500 MPa. Ec(40) = 4700√40 ≈ 29,725 MPa. Ratio: 29,725 / 23,500 ≈ 1.265 (rounded to 1.27). Beam A (lower E) deflects more[cite: 1].
rationale.takeaway: Deflection varies with the square root of concrete compressive strength[cite: 1].

questions.text: What is the formula for the Modulus of Elasticity of normal-weight concrete per NSCP 2015?

options.text: Ec = 4,700 × f'c (f'c in MPa)
Ec = 4,700√f'c (f'c in MPa)
Ec = 3,000√f'c (f'c in MPa)

rationale.a: The relationship is non-linear; it depends on the square root of f'c, not the direct value[cite: 1].
rationale.c: 3,000 is an incorrect coefficient; the code specifically mandates 4,700 for normal-weight concrete[cite: 1].
rationale.d: 0.003 is the assumed maximum usable strain at the extreme concrete compression fiber, not a factor for the modulus of elasticity[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: Per NSCP 2015 Section 419.2.2.1, the modulus of elasticity for concrete is calculated as 4,700 times the square root of the specified compressive strength[cite: 1].

questions.text: Define the Modulus of Rigidity (Shear Modulus) and explain its relationship to the Modulus of Elasticity.

options.text: G is the resistance to shear deformation; G ≈ E / 2 for most materials, indicating a proportional relationship
G is the resistance to shear deformation; G = E / (2(1 + ν)), where ν is Poisson's ratio
G is identical to E; they are interchangeable terms, which is a common misconception
G is always greater than E because shear resistance is stronger than normal resistance, which is incorrect

rationale.a: G ≈ E/2 is a very rough approximation; the exact formula includes the 1 + ν term[cite: 1].
rationale.c: E measures axial stiffness (normal stress/strain), whereas G measures shear stiffness[cite: 1].
rationale.d: Since Poisson's ratio for structural materials is positive (0.25 to 0.35), G is always significantly less than E[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: The shear modulus (G) represents the ratio of shear stress to shear strain. For isotropic materials, it is related to E and Poisson's ratio (ν) by G = E / [2(1+ν)][cite: 1].

questions.text: What does the Modulus of Resilience measure, and what is its relationship to the yield strength and Modulus of Elasticity?

options.text: The total energy absorbed from zero stress to rupture; UR = Fy² / (2E), which is crucial for understanding material toughness
The maximum elastic energy stored per unit volume without permanent deformation; UR = Fy² / (2E)
The material's ability to resist impact; UR = Fu / E, which is often used in dynamic loading scenarios
The stress level at which the material yields; UR = Fy, typically used in basic structural analysis

rationale.a: Energy absorbed up to rupture is the Modulus of Toughness, not Resilience[cite: 1].
rationale.c: Impact resistance is related to toughness and ductility, but the formula provided is incorrect[cite: 1].
rationale.d: Fy is the yield stress, which is a single point on the curve; resilience is the energy (area) accumulated up to that point[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: Resilience is the capacity of a material to absorb energy when it is deformed elastically. It is the area under the elastic portion of the stress-strain curve, calculated as UR = Fy² / (2E)[cite: 1].

questions.text: Two beams have identical dimensions and carry identical loads: one is made of steel (E = 200,000 MPa) and one of concrete (Ec ≈ 25,000 MPa). If the steel beam deflects 5 mm, what is the approximate deflection of the concrete beam?

options.text: 5 mm (same as steel)
20 mm (4 times more)
40 mm (8 times more)
0.625 mm (eight times less)

rationale.a: The beams have different materials; stiffness (E) dictates that their deflections will differ[cite: 1].
rationale.b: The ratio of E values is 8, not 4[cite: 1].
rationale.d: Concrete is less stiff than steel, so it must deflect more, not less[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: Deflection is inversely proportional to stiffness (E). The ratio of deflections is E_steel / E_concrete = 200,000 / 25,000 = 8. Thus, the concrete beam deflects 8 times more: 8 × 5 mm = 40 mm[cite: 1].
rationale.takeaway: Lower Modulus of Elasticity results in proportionally higher deflection[cite: 1].

questions.text: Explain the difference between Modulus of Resilience and Modulus of Toughness in terms of the stress-strain diagram regions they represent.

options.text: Resilience represents the entire stress-strain curve; Toughness represents only the elastic region, which is incorrect
Resilience represents only the elastic region (linear portion); Toughness represents the entire curve from origin to rupture
Both represent the same thing; they are synonymous measures of energy, which is a common misconception
Resilience measures material strength; Toughness measures axial stiffness, which is not accurate

rationale.c: They are different measures; toughness includes the much larger area of the plastic region[cite: 1].
rationale.d: Both are measures of energy density (energy per volume), not pure strength or stiffness[cite: 1].
rationale.correct: Resilience is the energy stored elastically (recoverable), whereas Toughness is the total energy absorbed by the material before it fractures (includes non-recoverable plastic deformation)[cite: 1].
rationale.takeaway: Toughness represents total energy capacity; Resilience represents elastic energy capacity[cite: 1].
